Introduction to MPI

# MPI Tutorial 1: Getting Started with MPI

Learning outcomes: compile, launch, inspect ranks, and exchange a value with MPI_Send and MPI_Recv

<!-- page: 2 -->

## What Will You Learn Today?

By the end of this tutorial, you should be able to:

Explain why MPI is useful for parallel computing

Compare shared-memory threads with MPI processes

Compile and launch one MPI program as multiple processes

Exchange data using MPI_Send and MPI_Recv

## Shared-Memory Threads

## Multiple threads execute within one process

Thread 0

Thread 1

Thread 2

Shared Memory

Shared address space — threads can access the same variables

Local execution state — each thread has its own stack

Synchronization — shared updates must be coordinated





Threads share memory; coordination is the main programming challenge.

<!-- page: 9 -->

## Why MPI Processes?

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_66_102_1935_1100.jpg" alt="Image" width="93%" /></div>


Scale Beyond One Machine

Processes can run across multiple hosts

Standard Communication Abstractions

Send / Recv / Broadcast / Reduce

Communication is explicit, but MPI hides low-level network details.

MPI combines private process memory with portable communication across one or many machines.

## One Program, Many MPI Processes

mpiexec -n <number of processes> <executable>

mpiexec -n 4 ./program

launch 4 processes

one executable

./program

Rank 0

same code, different rank

Rank 1

same code, different rank

Rank 2

same code, different rank

Rank 3

same code, different rank

Process: one independent MPI worker



Rank: process identifier inside a communicator

Size: number of processes in

that communicator

MPI_COMM_WORLD = default communicator

SPMD: every process runs the same program, but uses its rank to choose local work.

## MPI Program Lifecycle

MPI_Init(&argc, &argv);
1 Program Start
MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, &rank);
MPI_Comm_size(MPI_COMM_WORLD, &size);
/* local computation */
/* communication */
MPI_Finalize();
MPI calls occur after MPI_Init.
Every process executes the same program.

## Demo 1: Hello MPI

# Compile
$ mpicc hello.c -o hello

# Run
$ mpiexec -n 1 ./hello
$ mpiexec -n 4 ./hello

Hello from rank 0 of 4
Hello from rank 1 of 4
Hello from rank 2 of 4
Hello from rank 3 of 4

## Demo 2: Send / Recv in Code

## Core rank-specific branches after MPI initialization

if (rank == 0) {
    int x = 42;
    MPI_Send(&x, 1, MPI_INT, 1, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD);
} else if (rank == 1) {
    int x;
    MPI_Recv(&x, 1, MPI_INT, 0, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD, MPI_STATUS_IGNORE);
}
